why.core: Voting is how you get a say in who runs the country, the state and your local council. In Australia, you can **enrol from 16**, so you're ready the moment you turn 18. why.extend: Voting is compulsory for adult citizens in Australia, but you can only vote if you're enrolled. You can **enrol from 16**, so you're ready at 18. Getting it right means finding the official agency, reading its instructions closely and completing a government document accurately: civic literacy you'll use for the rest of your life.

articles.title: How to get on the roll

body.support:
Elections are run by special groups. The **AEC** runs federal elections. The **VEC** runs Victorian elections. Their websites end in **.gov.au**. They are the best place to get the facts.

To vote, your name must be on the **electoral roll**. That's the list of voters.

Voting is **compulsory** at 18. That means you must vote. But first you must **enrol**.

You can **enrol from 16**. Then you're ready at 18.

To enrol at **aec.gov.au/enrol**:

1. **Check** you are an Australian citizen and 16 or older.
2. **Get your ID ready.** A Medicare card works.
3. **Fill in the form.** Your name, birthday and address.
4. **Sign** to say it's true.

Moved house? **Update** it.

Heard something about voting in a group chat? Check the AEC website.
body.core:
In Australia, elections are run by independent agencies, not by politicians. The **AEC** (Australian Electoral Commission) runs federal elections. The **VEC** (Victorian Electoral Commission) runs state and council elections in Victoria. Their websites end in **.gov.au**. They're the best place for election facts: dates, how to enrol, where to vote.

To vote, your name has to be on the **electoral roll**: the official list of voters. Voting at federal elections has been **compulsory** since 1924. If you don't vote and have no good reason, you can be fined. But you can only vote if you've **enrolled**.

Here's the good part: you can **enrol from 16**. Then you're ready to vote as soon as you turn 18. In Victoria, **one form** enrols you for federal, state and council elections.

To enrol online at **aec.gov.au/enrol**:

1. **Check you're eligible**: an Australian citizen, aged 16 or older.
2. **Get your evidence of identity ready**: a Medicare card, driver licence, Australian passport or citizenship number. If you don't have any, someone who is already enrolled can confirm who you are.
3. **Fill in the form**: your full name, date of birth and the address where you live now.
4. **Sign the declaration** to say it's all true.

After that, keep it **up to date**. If you move house or change your name, update your enrolment.

Be careful where you get election information. Rumours spread fast in group chats and on social media. If it's about how, when or where to vote, check the AEC or VEC website.
body.extend:
Australian elections are run by independent agencies, not by governments or parties. The **AEC** (Australian Electoral Commission) runs federal elections and referendums. The **VEC** (Victorian Electoral Commission) runs state and council elections in Victoria. Their official websites are the sources to trust for dates, enrolment and voting.

You can only vote if your name is on the **electoral roll**. Enrolling and voting are both **compulsory** for eligible adults. Federal voting has been compulsory since 1924, and not voting without a valid reason can bring a fine.

You can **enrol from 16**, so you're ready to vote at 18. In Victoria, a single enrolment covers federal, state and council elections.

To enrol online at **aec.gov.au/enrol**:

1. **Check you're eligible**: an Australian citizen, aged 16 or over.
2. **Prepare evidence of identity**: a Medicare card, driver licence, Australian passport or citizenship number. Or an enrolled person can confirm who you are.
3. **Complete the form** carefully: full legal name, date of birth and the address where you live.
4. **Sign the declaration** that it's all true.

Then keep it **up to date** when you move or change your name.

False claims about voting spread fast. For how, when or where to vote, trust the AEC or VEC.

caseStudies.title: The missing young voters

body.support:
Before the 2025 election, the AEC counted who was on the roll. Almost everyone was: **98.2%**.

But young people aged **18 to 24** were behind. Only **92%** were on the roll.

That means about **160,000** young people could not vote. They were not on the roll.

More young people are enrolling every year. In 2021 it was **84.5%**. In 2024 it was **90.2%**.

The easy fix? Enrol at 16 or 17. Then you're ready at 18.
body.core:
Before every federal election, the AEC reports how many people are enrolled. In April 2025, before that year's election, it announced a **record**: **98.2%** of eligible Australians were on the roll.

But one group was behind: young people aged **18 to 24**. Their enrolment rate was **92.0%**.

That sounds high. But the AEC's own figures showed about **1,991,700** young people aged 18 to 24 who could enrol, and about **1,831,800** who had. That's roughly **160,000 young Australians** who couldn't vote, because they weren't on the roll.

The youth rate has been rising: it was **84.5%** in June 2021 and **90.2%** in June 2024. Every year, more young people are getting on the roll before they turn 18.

The easiest way not to be one of the missing? Enrol at 16 or 17. Then you're on the roll, ready to vote, the moment you turn 18.
body.extend:
Before each federal election, the AEC publishes enrolment statistics. In April 2025 it announced a **record national enrolment rate of 98.2%**, the third election in a row to set a record.

One group lagged: Australians aged **18 to 24**, with an enrolment rate of **92.0%**. The AEC's table put the eligible population of young people at about **1,991,700**, with about **1,831,800** enrolled. The gap is roughly **160,000 young people** without a vote.

The trend is improving. Youth enrolment was **84.5%** at June 2021 and **90.2%** at June 2024. Enrolling at 16 or 17, before you're eligible to vote, is one reason more young people are on the roll when an election is called.

The statistics raise a civic question worth discussing: why are young people the least likely to be enrolled, and whose job is it to change that?

**Our goal:** Get ten more students at our school on the roll this term.

**What we know:** You can enrol at 16 or 17, so you are ready to vote when you turn 18. It takes about five minutes on the AEC website.

**Our plan**
1. **Poster** near the canteen: “16 or older? Enrol in five minutes.” With a QR code to aec.gov.au/enrol.
2. **Lunchtime table** on Wednesday, with two laptops.
3. **What to bring:** ID, like a driver licence, a Medicare card or a passport.

**Who does what:** Jas makes the poster. Tom books the laptops. I talk to the Year 11 coordinator.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** federal — AEC; Victorian state — VEC; local council — VEC. Enrol from 16, so you're ready to vote at 18 and don't miss out. Evidence of identity: Medicare card, driver licence, Australian passport, citizenship number (or an enrolled person confirms who you are). Check the AEC or VEC website.

**Sort:** aec.gov.au — reliable; group chat rumour — check it; vec.vic.gov.au — reliable; vote by text — check it (it isn't true); party flyer — check it; Youth Central — reliable.

**Form:** 1 eligibility; 2 full name matching ID; 3 date of birth in the right order; 4 current address; 5 evidence of identity; 6 declaration (only sign if it's true).

**Steps (sample):** 1 Check you're an Australian citizen aged 16+. 2 Get your evidence of identity ready (or someone enrolled to confirm who you are). 3 Go to aec.gov.au/enrol and fill in your full name, date of birth and current address. 4 Sign the declaration. 5 Update your enrolment if you move.

**Case study:** youth enrolment was 92.0% (lowest of any group), about 160,000 not enrolled; possible reasons include not knowing you can enrol early, moving house often, not seeing it as urgent; the AEC runs the roll and publishes official data.

realityCheck: **Not every student can enrol.** Students who aren't Australian citizens can't enrol, and you shouldn't put anyone on the spot. Everyone can complete the practice form, and that fully counts.
**Keep enrolment private.** Never collect students' real details or screenshots of their enrolment. A student telling you they enrolled is enough.
**Stay politically neutral.** The course is about the process, not parties or issues. Follow your school's guidance on political neutrality.
**The detail.** The AEC allows enrolment from 16 for federal elections; the Victorian form notes that state enrolment starts at 17. One form covers both, so “enrol at 16” is the right message.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's short, practical and genuinely useful. Students who enrol often leave the lesson having done something adult for the first time.
